summary: An announcement of a tentative workshop on multi-site executive programs, which would let a user at any host or TIP command resources at many ARPANET sites through one conversational interface. The authors list the questions to discuss, including how resource interfaces could be standardized for server processes.

plainLanguage.summary: A meeting to plan one friendly control panel that lets you use many different computers on the network without learning each one's quirks.

subtitle: Announcement of a workshop on unified command interfaces for ARPANET resources

tldr.problem: Network users had to learn the specific commands and interfaces of each ARPANET host, making it difficult to access resources across different sites without becoming expert in multiple operating systems.
tldr.mechanism: Bob Thomas proposed a workshop to explore an ARPANET Executive: a standardized, conversational interface that would let users access resources across the network from any host. Key areas of discussion would include standardizing resource interfaces, establishing a common protocol, creating a common language for users, and enabling single-login access to multi-host resources.
tldr.outcome: The workshop (tentatively planned for April 1973) would explore whether such a unified interface was feasible and what architecture it should have. Experimental implementations like RSEXEC on TENEX demonstrated the concept.

facts.label: Workshop host
facts.value: BBN TENEX and BBN TIP groups

today: RFC 471 describes an early vision of unified multi-system access that foreshadowed modern concepts like single sign-on, distributed systems, and command-line interfaces across heterogeneous networks. The RSEXEC system mentioned was one of the first attempts at this abstraction. Modern systems like SSH, APIs, and distributed computing frameworks address these same concerns.

sections.title: The Need for a Common Interface
sections.content: Bob Thomas of BBN-TENEX announced a tentative workshop on multi-site executive programs. An executive program is one that accepts and interprets commands from a user and calls on other programs to provide needed resources. Thomas observed that the ARPANET community wanted to make diverse resources available to users through a standard, conversational facility called an ARPANET Executive. With such a facility, a user at any host or a TIP could conveniently access resources at other sites without needing to master each different host's operating system and command syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: Every computer on the network had its own weird way of doing things. The idea was to build a translator that everyone could use.

sections.title: Capabilities and Applications
sections.content: The ARPANET Executive could enable many services: locating a user by name anywhere on the network and establishing a teletype link for dialogue; providing status information on the subnet and all hosts; running an on-line ARPANET news service; maintaining on-line collections of trouble reports; and supporting practically unlimited additional services through a flexible framework. This vision anticipated many functions that would later be provided by email systems, web search, and messaging platforms.
sections.plainLanguage: With one control panel, you could find someone, send messages, check if computers were working, and read the news.

sections.title: Key Design Questions
sections.content: Thomas identified four major areas to address at the workshop. First, how could interfaces to diverse network resources be standardized so server processes could access them uniformly? Second, how could communication with such server processes be standardized, possibly through an ARPANET Executive protocol? Third, to what extent could the user-facing conversational interface be standardized, possibly through an ARPANET Executive language? Fourth, how could authentication and accounting be unified so a user could log in once and access resources at multiple sites?
sections.plainLanguage: The workshop would tackle four hard problems: making all computers understand the same commands, making a common language for them, protecting who can use what, and logging in just once.
